Genius Hacks Q3 2026 · Team TrustOps

TrustOps
FCRM Risk Assessment Workbench

Banks must assess every material change for AML, CFT and sanctions risk before it goes live. TrustOps turns that assessment into one traceable case: AI proposes with citations, people decide every item, and a deterministic engine calculates the score.

Divya Jain · Amey Phansalkar · Ayushi Gupta · Abhishek Pahuja · Vishal Wankhede · Ramesh Sen

FastAPI · React 19 · MongoDB 8 · RabbitMQ · Pydantic AI on Amazon Bedrock · OPA · OpenTelemetry · Claude Code

0:15 · openOne sentence on what it is, one on the stance: AI proposes, people decide, a deterministic engine calculates the score. Then move. The repository is the primary submission; this deck is the guided tour of our decisions.
Risk Assessment Workbench track

The problem as given

Change assessments lose time, vary by analyst and do not keep their reasoning

Context engineering · 10%

Submissions arrive incomplete

The business owner fills a form shaped by their own change, not by what the assessment needs. Gaps surface one question at a time over email, so most of an assessment’s duration is spent waiting on answers, not assessing.

Two analysts reach two answers

Policy is looked up from scratch each time, control effectiveness is judged from experience with no evidence required, and scoring runs in personal spreadsheets that drift apart. The outcome depends on who picked the case up.

The reasoning does not survive

The decision is recorded; the thinking behind it lives in email threads, local files and memory. When an examiner asks months later why a change was approved, the answer has to be rebuilt by hand.

Each is easy to fix alone, and each fix damages the other two. Faster means less checking, so answers vary more. Uniform means more mandatory steps, so cases take longer. Full records mean more writing for everyone.

Why it matters

A slow process gets routed around. Changes go undeclared or launch first, and a risk function nobody uses sees nothing.
A weak assessment becomes a systemic finding. After an incident, the question is whether the bank’s own process should have caught it.
Inconsistency means the control is not a control. Low-risk changes are over-assessed and risky ones slip through, in the same team, the same week.
Reasoning that cannot be retrieved cannot be defended. An outcome with no record of why can only be asserted.
0:35 · the problemBefore the build, the problem. Three failures in how change assessment runs today: incomplete submissions, inconsistent analysts, lost reasoning. The point to land is the tension: fixing one makes the others worse, so a fix has to address all three together. Next: how we turned that into a specification.
Track brief · docs/requirements/spec.md

01 · How we expanded the requirements

The brief left four decisions open. Research, business rules and routing rules closed them

Context engineering · 10%Engineering judgement · 5%

Research · 8 notes

Done before any build, from the use case text alone.

  • We mapped how assessment runs today, studied the frameworks it has to meet, and drew up a mock flow of how it should run.
  • We built a mock prototype first, to test that flow and iterate on it before any real code.
  • We also generated the test data: 197 sample policy clauses from nine sources, and 80 mock cases.

Business rules · 8

Rules that always apply, whatever the AI proposes. For example:

  • An AI model never writes a number. Scores, routing and the vote count are done by code.
  • Nothing is accepted in bulk. Every proposal is confirmed one at a time, and changing one needs a reason.
  • The product owner never sees a score.

Routing rules · 6, R1 to R6

Code applies these after every score to decide who handles the case. For example:

  • R1 lets the analyst close lower-risk cases (Band 1 and 2) and sends higher-risk ones (Band 3 and 4) to a committee vote.
  • R4 flags a case that may qualify for the fast lane. R5 assigns the case to an analyst.

What they decided

0:55 · flow, agents, gatesOne case, left to right. Colour is the point: green proposes, yellow decides, blue computes. The owner uploads, the intake agent proposes, the owner confirms each value. Code triages. The research and assessment agents propose, and the critic checks them on a different model. The analyst reviews item by item and only then does the engine score. The committee votes hidden, or the analyst closes a lower band. Nine agents and 18 gates fit into this one table, and none of the gates is a bulk accept. Hand off: rules on paper do not enforce themselves, so next is the architecture that does.

02 · Harness architecture

Services own state, Caseflow owns the sequence, agents only propose

AI harness and orchestration · 30%Production readiness · 5%

Transactional outbox

State, audit record and event are written together. The relay publishes later, at least once; consumers tolerate redelivery.

No HTTP inside a transaction

Caseflow enqueues a step with the transition and runs it outside. Steps are idempotent; S4 and S5 writes carry an idempotency key.

Contracts first

One contracts package; 112 API paths in the committed OpenAPI export; the web's route test fails on any path the export lacks.

02 · State of the AI

Six levels, each built on the one before: from reliable calls to audit and operations

AI harness and orchestration · 30%Human-in-the-loop · 15%

Level 1

Reliable calls

  • Strict output formats, extra fields refused
  • Timeouts per tier
  • One retry on the backup model, error shown
  • Broken or cut answers repaired in the run
  • Safe re-runs: idempotent steps, leases, outbox

Level 2

Cost control

  • Four model tiers, cheapest that passes its gate
  • One call per agent, no open loop
  • Tool calls capped at 0 or 1
  • Budgets from measured p90; case cap 250k
  • Prompt caching; oversized inputs split

Level 3

Seven guardrails

  • 1 Input scan · 2 Tool permits · 3 Budget
  • 4 Output check · 5 Rules as code
  • 6 Critic on another model
  • 7 Human gate
  • Every call crosses all seven

Level 4

Humans in charge

  • Nothing approved or rejected automatically
  • 18 human gates, each with its risk
  • A reason on every override and vote
  • Analyst handoff when the AI fails twice
  • Scores written only by code

Level 5

Proof it works

  • Nine test sets, one per agent
  • 27 deterministic checks plus an AI judge
  • 8 of 9 gates pass, live on Bedrock
  • A prompt cannot change without eval evidence
  • 12 kill-and-restart drills pass

Level 6

Audit and ops

  • Hash-chained audit, every decision recorded
  • Versions pinned per case for life
  • Live dashboards over OpenTelemetry
  • Token and cost tracking per case
  • Model registry in one file

03 · People, AI and gates

Three lanes. AI proposes, a person decides, code scores and routes

Human-in-the-loop and governance · 15%Engineering judgement · 5%

review_itemRisk: accepting an AI proposal unreadPer item; no bulk-accept endpoint exists. An override needs a reason and recomputes the score.
completenessRisk: reviewing on missing or contradictory inputsOne batched clarification round before review, so the analyst clock pauses once.
voteRisk: anchoring on colleagues' votesHidden until all three are cast; rationale required; one vote per member per round, unique in the database.
Deterministic by decisionRisk: a model writing a numberScores, routing, tally, release checks and chain verification are code. 9.8 to 10.4 after one override is a unit test. The PO never sees a score.

Why this chain

  • The cheapest model that passes its gate, per tier, with a fallback from another vendor family where the gate allows it.
  • The critic and the judges run on a different family than the assessor they check.
  • A model change needs a verified price row, an ADR and live eval evidence; the baseline describes only the chain it was measured on.
ai/models/tiers.yaml · tests/unit/ai/models/test_tier_chains.py · ADR-04, ADR-62, ADR-65

Appendix D · Decisions to expect

Each has an ADR row with the reason, what it gives us and what it supersedes

ADR-07Caseflow calls the scoring engine after proposals land; the assessment agent has no scoring tool. Rule 1 is strongest when no agent can reach the engine.
ADR-14Agent retry: attempt 1 on a fallback chain; attempt 2 on the fallback alone with the validation error appended; a second failure opens the handoff gate.
ADR-27Agents call live Bedrock only; replay and mock modes removed. The goldens are proved by unit tests, a live run prints its own numbers.
ADR-28No HTTP inside a consumer transaction: steps are enqueued through the outbox and run outside, idempotent by step id.
ADR-29The corpus and documents are synthetic and say so; 193 of 197 clauses were generated once with provenance tags. A verbatim quote is verbatim from stored text.
ADR-32The PO fence has three layers that trust none of the others: models without the fields, a role filter with a type-prefix blocklist, and a text scan.
ADR-59A live model call is a human gate for the build itself: nothing that calls Bedrock runs without the operator's approval, with an estimate at verified prices.
ADR-62 / 65No Opus in any chain; Nova Pro as judge with a 28k budget from one observation; Sonnet 5.5 on mid and strong with effort low.
ADR-72OpenObserve is the one observability store; Jaeger, Prometheus and Grafana removed to cut the stack to what is read.
ADR-76Every citation chip opens its source: the anchored page and line of the upload, the PDF itself, or the clause text.
ADR-77 / 80 / 81Oversized inputs are split inside the worker and merged by code; output allowance is computed per request and broken answers repaired; the strong tier gets 56k per attempt and a case 250k.
ADR-82A critic's precedent-deviation finding is checked by code against the assessment and the same precedent search before it can become a review item.

Also in the log: why RabbitMQ over Redis as the bus (ADR-02), why AWS everywhere (ADR-03), why the prototype contributed design tokens only (ADR-06), why a 1-1-1 committee split never auto-defers (ADR-31), and why the web's route names became the API contract (ADR-30).
